analysis.investment_thesis: ICICI Prudential AMC is a genuinely exceptional business — 75%+ operating margins, 103% ROCE, and 32% earnings CAGR — but the Magic Formula explicitly excludes financial companies, and even setting that aside, the earnings yield of ~2.6% (EBIT ₹3,635 Cr / EV ~₹142,185 Cr) is catastrophically below the 12% threshold. Paying 56x earnings for a great business is not the Magic Formula way.
key_strengths: Exceptional ROCE of 103.4% — capital-light fee business with near-zero tangible assets required
Operating margins of 75%+ sustained across all three years with strong revenue CAGR (~36% over 2Y)
FCF conversion is strong: ₹2,162 Cr FCF vs ₹2,651 Cr net profit (81%), minimal debt (D/E 0.04)
key_risks: Earnings yield of ~2.6% (EBIT/EV) is 5x below the Magic Formula's minimum threshold of 12% — the stock is priced for perfection
Financial company: Greenblatt explicitly excludes AMCs/financials because capital structure distorts the two core Magic Formula metrics
AUM-linked revenue makes earnings cyclically exposed to equity market corrections — a 30% market drawdown could compress revenues sharply at a 56x multiple
red_flags: Earnings yield ~2.6% — far below the 6% floor where the Magic Formula even begins to consider a stock
P/E of 56x and EV/EBITDA of 32x leave zero margin of safety for any earnings miss or market derating
2025 capex spike to ₹412 Cr vs ₹55 Cr in 2024 — needs explanation; could signal one-time item or growing capital intensity
analysis.detailed_analysis:
ICICI Prudential AMC sits in an odd position under the Magic Formula framework: it is precisely the kind of business Greenblatt would admire (durable competitive moat, minimal capital requirements, stellar returns on the capital deployed) but it fails both mandatory tests. First, it is a financial services company and Greenblatt explicitly excludes these from ranking — EBIT/EV and EBIT/(NWC+NFA) lose meaning when the business model is managing other people's money rather than deploying its own. Second, even applying the formula mechanically, the earnings yield is approximately 2.6% (FY2025 EBIT of ₹3,635 Cr against an EV of ~₹142,185 Cr), roughly one-fifth of the 12% threshold that characterizes a cheap stock. The Magic Formula only rewards cheapness AND quality simultaneously; this stock offers quality without cheapness.

The business fundamentals are genuinely impressive — revenue compounded at ~36% over two years, operating margins expanded from 75% to 75.3%, and FCF grew from ₹1,359 Cr to ₹2,162 Cr. The 87.6% promoter holding (ICICI Bank + Prudential) provides stability but also limits float. However, at 56x trailing earnings, the market has already fully priced in multiple years of future growth. A value investor paying this multiple is left with no margin of safety if AUM growth slows, markets correct, or the regulatory environment for mutual fund expense ratios tightens further — all real risks in the Indian AMC space. This is a stock to admire, not to buy today.
